questions.prompt: Which data structure is most commonly used in Swift interviews to represent a sparse graph?

options.text: An adjacency list dictionary mapping vertices to neighbor arrays.
options.explanation: An adjacency list like [Int: [Int]] stores only existing edges, taking O(V + E) space.

options.text: A full two-dimensional Boolean matrix allocating V squared cells.
options.explanation: An adjacency matrix consumes O(V^2) space, which wastes memory for sparse graphs.

options.text: A singly linked list holding vertices without neighbor pointers.
options.explanation: A simple linked list cannot represent branching edge connections efficiently.

options.text: A maximum priority queue sorted by alphabetical vertex names.
options.explanation: A priority queue does not store graph connectivity or edge lists.

questions.prompt: Why is a visited Set required when searching a graph with BFS or DFS?

options.text: To serialize graph vertices into an encoded binary file format.
options.explanation: A visited set tracks traversal progress, not disk persistence.

options.text: To prevent infinite loops caused by cycles and repeated visits.
options.explanation: Graphs can contain cycles. Without tracking visited nodes, traversals can loop forever.

options.text: To keep all vertex values sorted in ascending numerical order.
options.explanation: A Set does not preserve or enforce numerical sorted order.

options.text: To avoid heap allocations on Swift standard collection types.
options.explanation: Sets allocate heap storage for their internal hash table buckets.

questions.prompt: What graph algorithm finds the minimum number of edges between two nodes in an unweighted graph?

options.text: Depth-first search with post-order traversal.
options.explanation: DFS explores deep paths first and does not guarantee shortest path in unweighted graphs.

options.text: Binary search on sorted adjacency keys.
options.explanation: Binary search finds items in a sorted array, not shortest paths in graphs.

options.text: Breadth-first search using a first-in first-out queue.
options.explanation: BFS explores nodes in increasing order of distance, guaranteeing the shortest path.

options.text: Kruskal minimum spanning tree construction.
options.explanation: Kruskal algorithm builds minimum spanning trees on weighted graphs, not shortest path.

questions.prompt: How do you represent an undirected edge between vertices u and v in an adjacency list?

options.text: Add v to u list only, because edges are assumed symmetric.
options.explanation: Adjacency lists are directed by default; omitting u from v leaves the reverse path missing.

options.text: Insert a negative edge weight into a separate priority queue.
options.explanation: Negative weights do not model undirected edge connectivity.

options.text: Create a new root vertex pointing to both u and v.
options.explanation: Graphs do not require artificial root nodes for undirected connections.

options.text: Append v to u neighbor list AND append u to v neighbor list.
options.explanation: An undirected edge allows two-way traversal, so both vertices must list each other.

questions.prompt: What is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)?

options.text: A directed graph that contains no closed directed cycles.
options.explanation: A DAG has directed edges and no path exists from any node back to itself.

options.text: An undirected graph where every vertex has an even degree.
options.explanation: DAGs are strictly directed, not undirected, and degree parity is unrelated.

options.text: A tree where every parent node has exactly two children.
options.explanation: That defines a binary tree, which is only a very narrow subset of DAGs.

options.text: A graph with identical positive weights on every single edge.
options.explanation: A DAG can be unweighted or have varied weights; acyclic structure is the key.

questions.prompt: In Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting, which vertices are placed into the initial queue?

options.text: Vertices with the largest total number of outgoing edges.
options.explanation: Out-degree does not determine readiness in dependency resolution.

options.text: Vertices with an in-degree of zero, having no dependencies.
options.explanation: Vertices with in-degree 0 have no incoming prerequisites and can be processed immediately.

options.text: Vertices that belong to the largest detected cycle component.
options.explanation: Cyclic nodes cannot have in-degree 0 until incoming dependencies are resolved.

options.text: Vertices whose numerical ID matches the root level zero index.
options.explanation: Any vertex with in-degree 0 qualifies, regardless of its numerical index value.

questions.prompt: How does Kahn's algorithm detect if a directed graph has a cycle?

options.text: It checks if the queue throws an out-of-bounds index error.
options.explanation: A queue drains normally without index exceptions during Kahn's algorithm.

options.text: It verifies whether edge weights sum to a negative number.
options.explanation: Kahn's algorithm operates on DAG structure regardless of edge weights.

options.text: The count of processed nodes is less than the total node count.
options.explanation: Nodes within a directed cycle never reach in-degree 0, so the processed count is below V.

options.text: The algorithm restarts the queue with all leaf vertices.
options.explanation: The algorithm terminates when the queue empties; it does not automatically restart.

questions.prompt: What is the primary trade-off of an adjacency matrix compared to an adjacency list?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: It requires recursive function calls for every read access.
options.explanation: Matrix lookups are direct array subscript indexing operations.

options.text: It cannot store weighted values or floating-point weights.
options.explanation: An adjacency matrix can store any numeric weight in its cells.

options.text: It prevents thread-safe mutations in Swift 6 concurrency.
options.explanation: Concurrency safety depends on synchronization, not matrix representation.

options.text: It gives O(1) edge lookups but consumes O(V squared) memory.
options.explanation: Checking matrix[u][v] is instantaneous O(1), but allocating V x V cells uses quadratic space.

questions.prompt: How should a graph search algorithm visit every node when the graph is disconnected?

options.text: Loop through all vertices 0..<V and start traversal from unvisited ones.
options.explanation: An outer loop over all vertex IDs guarantees that separate components are not missed.

options.text: Connect all disconnected vertices to node zero with artificial edges.
options.explanation: Adding fake edges changes the topology and invalidates path and cycle properties.

options.text: Run binary search to find the missing disconnected components.
options.explanation: Binary search requires sorted arrays, not disconnected graph topologies.

options.text: Throw a fatal error because disconnected graphs are invalid inputs.
options.explanation: Disconnected graphs are completely valid and frequent in real-world problems.

questions.prompt: What real-world iOS developer workflow relies directly on DAG topological sorting?

options.text: Auto Layout constraint solving using linear equations.
options.explanation: Auto Layout uses the Cassowary linear programming solver, not topological sorting.

options.text: Swift Package Manager and Xcode build target dependency ordering.
options.explanation: Packages and framework targets declare dependencies forming a DAG resolved via topological sort.

options.text: SwiftUI view diffing and rendering tree reconciliation.
options.explanation: SwiftUI view reconciliation operates on hierarchy trees, not general DAG topological sorting.

options.text: Core Data SQLite schema migration index hashing.
options.explanation: SQLite index hashing uses b-trees and hashing rather than DAG topological sort.

questions.prompt: In three-color DFS cycle detection for directed graphs, what does hitting a gray (visiting) node mean?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: The node has completed all child searches and has no cycle.
options.explanation: That describes a black (visited/finished) node, not a gray node.

options.text: The node is disconnected from the rest of the directed graph.
options.explanation: A disconnected node starts in white (unvisited) state.

options.text: A back-edge was found pointing to an active ancestor, revealing a cycle.
options.explanation: A gray node is currently on the recursion call stack; reaching it again confirms a cycle.

options.text: The graph is guaranteed to be a valid bipartite layout.
options.explanation: Gray state in three-color DFS identifies active recursion ancestors, not bipartite sets.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS on a graph represented as an adjacency list?

options.text: O(V squared) time, regardless of edge density.
options.explanation: O(V^2) applies to adjacency matrix representations, not adjacency lists.

options.text: O(log V) time, using binary subdivision.
options.explanation: Graph traversals must inspect vertices and edges, which cannot be done in log time.

options.text: O(E squared) time, because edges are compared pairwise.
options.explanation: Traversals visit each edge at most twice in undirected graphs, taking linear edge time.

options.text: O(V + E) time, visiting every vertex and traversing every edge.
options.explanation: Each vertex is queued or pushed once, and each outgoing edge is examined once or twice.

questions.prompt: How do you detect cycles in an undirected graph using DFS traversal?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: If a visited neighbor is encountered that is not the immediate parent node.
options.explanation: Because edges are bidirectional, the parent is already visited; any other visited neighbor indicates a cycle.

options.text: If any vertex has an odd number of outgoing edge connections.
options.explanation: Odd vertex degree does not indicate cyclic graph structure.

options.text: If the topological sort output contains negative in-degree values.
options.explanation: Topological sort requires directed acyclic graphs and is not used on undirected graphs.

options.text: If the BFS queue length exceeds the total number of graph vertices.
options.explanation: Queue length is bounded by vertex count and does not signal cycles.

questions.prompt: When should Dijkstra's algorithm be chosen instead of standard breadth-first search?

options.text: When the graph has unweighted edges of uniform length one.
options.explanation: BFS is faster (O(V+E)) than Dijkstra for unweighted graphs.

options.text: When edges have varied non-negative costs or travel weights.
options.explanation: BFS only handles uniform unweighted edges; Dijkstra finds shortest paths with non-negative weights.

options.text: When the graph contains negative weight cycles.
options.explanation: Dijkstra fails on graphs with negative weights; Bellman-Ford must be used.

options.text: When the graph is guaranteed to be a balanced binary tree.
options.explanation: Trees do not require Dijkstra shortest path algorithms.

questions.prompt: How can a 2D grid of rows and columns be modeled as a graph in iOS interview questions?

options.text: By inserting each row as an AVL tree and sorting columns.
options.explanation: Grid problems do not require AVL tree structures.

options.text: By converting all grid coordinates to hexadecimal string keys.
options.explanation: String conversions introduce overhead; coordinate tuples (r, c) or flat indices are standard.

options.text: Each cell is a vertex, and adjacent horizontal/vertical cells form edges.
options.explanation: In grid problems (like number of islands), cells are nodes and 4-way adjacent valid cells are edges.

options.text: Grids cannot be processed using graph algorithms in Swift.
options.explanation: Grid problems are classic implicit graph traversal problems.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, compare an adjacency list and an adjacency matrix. Mention time and space complexity differences and provide an example of when you would choose each representation.

rubric.criterion: Compares space complexity: O(V + E) for adjacency list vs O(V^2) for adjacency matrix
Compares edge lookup time: O(degree(u)) for list vs O(1) for matrix
Provides clear scenarios for each (sparse graphs/interviews for list, dense graphs/instant lookup for matrix)

questions.modelAnswer: An adjacency list stores neighbors in a dictionary or array of lists, taking O(V + E) space. An adjacency matrix allocates a 2D array taking O(V squared) space. While a matrix checks edge existence in O(1) time, an adjacency list is much more memory efficient for sparse graphs. In iOS coding interviews, an adjacency list is almost always preferred.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why graph traversals require a visited Set while tree traversals usually do not. Describe what happens if the visited set is omitted when searching a cyclic graph.

rubric.criterion: Explains that trees are hierarchical and acyclic with a single root
Explains that graphs can contain cycles and multiple paths to the same node
Explains that omitting visited causes infinite loops or stack overflow crashes

questions.modelAnswer: A tree is an acyclic hierarchy where each node has exactly one parent, so each node is visited only once without cycles. Graphs can contain cycles and multiple distinct paths connecting the same vertices. Without a visited Set, BFS or DFS will repeatedly re-enqueue or revisit cyclic vertices, causing an infinite loop or a stack overflow crash.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, describe how Kahn's algorithm detects circular dependencies using in-degrees. Explain why cyclic nodes fail to enter the processing queue.

rubric.criterion: Explains computing in-degrees and seeding the queue with nodes having in-degree 0
Explains that nodes inside a cycle depend on each other, so their in-degrees never reach zero
Concludes that a processed count less than V confirms the presence of a cycle

questions.modelAnswer: Kahn's algorithm begins by counting incoming dependencies (in-degrees) and enqueuing nodes with in-degree zero. As each node is dequeued, in-degrees of its neighbors are decremented by one. If a cycle exists, nodes in that cycle continually depend on one another, preventing their in-degrees from ever dropping to zero. Consequently, the total count of processed nodes will be less than V, confirming a cycle.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how to handle disconnected components in a graph search problem. Describe the outer loop pattern and why starting only from node zero fails.

rubric.criterion: Explains that starting only from node 0 fails because edges do not cross disconnected components
Explains using an outer loop iterating over all vertex indices from 0 to V - 1
Explains checking the visited set before launching BFS or DFS from each vertex

questions.modelAnswer: A graph may consist of several disconnected subgraphs with no edges between them. Starting a search only from node 0 leaves all nodes in other components unvisited. To handle this, write an outer loop iterating through all vertices from 0 to V minus 1. For each vertex not yet in the visited Set, launch a new BFS or DFS traversal, incrementing a component counter.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain the three-color DFS cycle detection algorithm for directed graphs. Describe what the three colors represent and what triggers cycle detection.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Defines the three states (white = unvisited, gray = visiting / on call stack, black = visited / done)
Explains that encountering a gray node indicates a back-edge and confirms a directed cycle
Explains marking nodes black once all adjacent edges have been processed

questions.modelAnswer: The three-color DFS method tracks three node states: white (unvisited), gray (currently in the recursion call stack), and black (fully explored). When exploring neighbors, if DFS encounters a node that is currently gray, it has reached an ancestor on the current path. This back-edge confirms the existence of a directed cycle. When all neighbors of a node finish without cycles, the node transitions to black.
